evals.prompt: I run partnerships at Hadleigh Forms (B2B form-automation SaaS, about $6M ARR, self-serve to $99/mo then sales-assisted). We launched a referral partner program 14 months ago: 62 signed partners, 5 of them have ever sent us a deal, and the only two deals that closed both came from the same person. My VP wants to add an affiliate program next quarter because it's basically the same plumbing and costs us almost nothing. Give me a 12-month partner category roadmap. First result has to land by end of Q2 and I have no new headcount coming.
evals.expected_output: A roadmap whose stage 1 is finishing the unproven referral motion rather than adding a category, with the 8% activation read as a stop-recruiting signal, the affiliate ask refused or gated, capacity and deadline treated as caps, and evidence-based gates plus a Not now list with re-entry triggers.
expectations: States the referral motion is not yet a minimum viable ecosystem (MVE) because it has no repeatable joint wins, only one partner producing.
Computes or states the referral cohort's activation rate as roughly 8% (5 of 62).
States that activation below roughly 20% means stop recruiting and fix enablement, not recruit harder.
Makes stage 1 of the roadmap finishing or fixing the existing referral motion rather than adding a new category.
Declines to open an affiliate category in stage 1, or gates it explicitly behind the referral motion's gate.
Rejects 'it is cheap and reuses the same plumbing' as a sufficient reason to add a category, stating that cheapest and most efficient are different orderings.
Treats the end-of-Q2 date as a re-ranking input that promotes fast-acting categories and rules out any category whose first revenue arrives after that date.
Names the no-new-headcount constraint as a capacity cap on the roadmap, not as a detail to work around.
Attaches kill criteria that include an activation floor and a time-to-first-deal window.
States that every stage gate opens on evidence, never on a calendar date alone.
Places at least one category in a 'Not now' list with an explicit re-entry trigger.
Carries a provenance flag on any external benchmark quoted, for example flagging the sub-20% unmanaged activation floor as vendor-sourced.

evals.prompt: Norberg Ledger, B2B accounting-automation platform, $14M ARR, mid-market. Live today: a referral track (35 partners, 44% activation, joint wins repeating across at least 9 different partners) and nothing else. We have a documented public API, multi-tenant architecture, a sandbox, and 4 integrations customers built themselves without any help from us. Capacity: 2 partner managers, one enablement writer, $400k program budget for the year. Leadership's instinct is to just widen referral into a bigger affiliate network because it's the cheapest thing we could do. What should we actually add next, and in what order over 24 months?
evals.expected_output: A 24-month sequence opening with a formalized technology/ISV category, justified by the efficiency order and by the integration surface making a later marketplace stage cheap, with capacity numbers fixed before sequencing and at least one category deleted with a re-entry trigger.
expectations: Recommends formalizing the technology/ISV category as the first added stage.
States the B2B efficiency order explicitly, with tech/ISV ahead of referral/affiliate (tech/ISV > referral/affiliate > agency > marketplace > MSP == SI/GSI > reseller/VAR).
Explains that referral/affiliate is the cheapest category but not the most efficient one, because nothing it builds makes the next category cheaper.
States that the ISV integration surface is reused by a later marketplace stage, and by agencies or MSPs, which is what makes those stages cheaper.
Names the 4 customer-built integrations as existing uncompensated third-party activity and the cheapest thing to formalize.
Confirms the referral motion already qualifies as a proven MVE (44% activation, repeatable joint wins) so stage 1 need not be finishing it.
Sequences any marketplace stage after the ISV stage, not before it.
Fixes capacity numbers (partner-manager-to-partner ratios, enablement bandwidth, budget) before presenting a sequence.
Opens one stage at a time, allowing at most two in parallel and only when they share enablement infrastructure, stated explicitly.
Sets each stage's gate threshold as repeatable joint wins across multiple partners, not a single first win.
Deletes or defers at least one category from the pool with the constraint that ruled it out and a re-entry trigger.
Does not recommend reseller/VAR as an early stage, and if it is discussed, names its structurally collapsed margin.

evals.prompt: Board slide says 'launch MSP tier, sign two global SIs, and stand up a reseller channel' within the next 12 months. Reality at Kestrel Vault (B2B backup and disaster-recovery software, $9M ARR, sales-led, average ACV $38k): I am the entire partnerships team. One person. We do have an ISV motion that's real, 11 integration partners and 6 of them actively sourcing. Nothing else exists. Product has no multi-tenant admin console and it is not on the roadmap. Sequence this honestly for me.
evals.expected_output: A sequence that deletes all three board categories from the candidate pool on capacity and readiness grounds, each recorded in Not now with a re-entry trigger, and proposes something the single-manager capacity can actually carry off the proven ISV base.
expectations: Deletes MSP, SI/GSI and reseller/VAR from the candidate pool rather than scheduling them later in the same year.
States that a partner team of one cannot carry a standing-job category and the proven motion at the same time.
Names the missing multi-tenant administration as a readiness prerequisite failure that independently rules out MSP.
Records each deleted category in a 'Not now' section with the specific constraint that ruled it out.
Gives each deleted category a named re-entry trigger, such as multi-tenant administration landing on the product roadmap or a second partner manager being hired.
Refuses to park the ruled-out categories at the bottom of a ranked list, stating that a demoted category reappears later as scope.
Identifies the ISV motion as the proven base and builds adjacency from it.
Proposes at least one category the current capacity can actually carry instead of the board's three.
States explicit capacity numbers (manager-to-partner ratio, enablement bandwidth) as the cap on the roadmap.
Notes that 'sign two global SIs' names companies rather than a category, so it is not a category decision.
States that the efficiency order starves SI/GSI and MSP despite their high value, and names the condition that would promote them.
Frames the roadmap as a reasoned, gated bet rather than a validated formula.

evals.prompt:
Reviewing this before it goes to our exec team Thursday. Company is Loomis Metrics, B2B analytics, $22M ARR.

PARTNER STRATEGY 2027
Q1: launch reseller program - industry data shows partners drive 28% of revenue
Q2: sign 3 GSIs, launch MSP tier
Q3: two hyperscaler marketplace listings + affiliate program
Q4: 220 total partners, partnerships = 20% of pipeline
Framing: Horizon 1 core resellers, Horizon 2 services, Horizon 3 ecosystem platform

Tighten this up for me, mainly the dates. I think Q2 is too aggressive.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to tune the dates, followed by a line-by-line teardown naming the missing capacity numbers, the calendar gates, the unflagged analyst figure, the logo-count target, the three-horizons force-fit, the reseller-first prerequisite failure and the missing conflict check, then a rebuild from the MVE and capacity up.
expectations: Refuses to fix the plan by adjusting quarter dates, and rebuilds it from the MVE and the capacity numbers instead.
Names the complete absence of capacity numbers (who manages, enables and supports each cohort) as the plan's central defect.
Names recruiting ahead of enablement as the failure this plan schedules in advance.
Rejects McKinsey's three horizons as a force-fit borrowed from innovation-portfolio planning that supplies vocabulary but no sequencing logic.
States that the three-horizons framing is standing where a gate structure should be, so no stage in the plan can fail.
Rejects the 220-partner target as logo counting and replaces it with activation, time-to-first-deal and partner-sourced pipeline.
Flags '28% of revenue' as an analyst figure describing mature programs, irrelevant to a company launching resellers next quarter.
Attaches a provenance flag to that 28% figure if it is kept at all (Forrester, ANALYST).
Identifies every stage as calendar-gated and replaces the quarter triggers with evidence thresholds.

Identifies reseller-first as placing the highest-prerequisite transact category first, and names the prerequisites the plan never mentions: deal registration, margin structure, certification, support model.
Notes that the efficiency order puts reseller/VAR last and that the plan states no buyer-route reason that would promote it.
Points out that 'sign 3 GSIs' is a named-company goal rather than a category decision, and that SI/GSI is the slowest, highest-load category.
Names the missing channel conflict check for the reseller, MSP and marketplace categories that all overlap the direct motion.

evals.prompt: Building the justification slide for our partner expansion ask at Brightmoor Signal (B2B security operations platform, $19M ARR). Numbers I want to use: buyers now complete 68% of their journey digitally so we need influence partners; 95% of Microsoft's revenue flows through partners; mature programs get 28% of company revenue through partnerships; and around 25% of the channel struggles to break even so we should stay away from resellers. We'll target 35% activation on the new category in year one. Sanity-check these for me and tell me what to put in the deck.
evals.expected_output: A provenance audit of each quoted number, identifying the 68% figure as a revised 2013 statistic Forrester itself called a myth, the 95% as Microsoft's own 2019 self-report, the break-even figure as superseded by the Omdia survey, with flags on everything surviving into the deck and the activation target rebuilt from the company's own base rates.
expectations: Flags the 68% digital-journey figure as derived from a 2013 SiriusDecisions statistic that Forrester itself later publicly called a myth and revised to '70-80% self-directed'.
States that the direction of that figure may hold but its precision does not, and refuses to present it as settled fact.

Traces the 95% Microsoft figure to Microsoft's own 2019 statement (Q2 FY2019 earnings commentary or corporate blog) and presents it as one company's self-reported commercial-revenue framing, not a current industry constant.
Flags the 28% mature-program revenue share as ANALYST (Forrester) and notes it describes mature programs.

States the '~25% of the channel struggles to break even' figure is superseded, and gives the current Omdia 378-partner survey figures: 58% expecting profit decline, 51% forecasting double-digit drops.
Attaches an explicit provenance flag to every benchmark that survives into the deck.
Uses or names the flag taxonomy consistently (ACADEMIC, ANALYST, VENDOR, VENDOR-COMMISSIONED, CONSULTANT, MIXED).
States that any number appearing in the roadmap without a provenance flag is a defect to fix before shipping.
Warns that nearly every published benchmark in this field comes from a party that profits when the number looks good, so vendor figures are directional context and never proof.
Tells the user to set the 35% activation target from their own existing categories' base rates, using published figures only to sanity-check.
Identifies academic alliance-portfolio research as the only independent, non-self-interested evidence base in this field.
Warns against comparing a vendor benchmark to a cohort measuring something different, naming signed partners versus active partners as the classic mismatch.

evals.prompt: Verrill & Co, DTC skincare, $18M revenue, 92% of it through our own site. We have an affiliate program (coupon and cashback sites mostly, roughly $1.1M attributed last year) and nothing else. Growth has been flat at about 4% year over year for three quarters. Everyone here wants to go after Target and Ulta next year because that's the biggest step available to us. Our founder has zero appetite for a standing job: she wants the first new channel producing within five months and won't fund permanent headcount. What's the category roadmap?
evals.expected_output: A B2C sequence opening with creator/influencer, deleting retail/wholesale and distributor on the stated effort ceiling while acknowledging flattened DTC growth as a genuine but overridden promotion condition, with incrementality as the sequencing driver and a cannibalization check on any overlapping route.
expectations: States the B2C efficiency order with creator/influencer first (creator/influencer > affiliate > marketplace > retail/wholesale > licensing == co-branding > distributor).
Recommends creator/influencer as the first added category.
Deletes retail/wholesale and distributor from the candidate pool because the stated effort ceiling excludes a standing job and permanent headcount.
Records retail/wholesale in 'Not now' with a named re-entry trigger, such as headcount approved or a retail buyer arriving inbound.
Acknowledges that flattened DTC growth is a genuine condition that would otherwise promote retail/wholesale, and names which constraint overrides it here.
Names the five-month deadline as the input promoting fast-acting categories and ruling out any whose first revenue arrives later.
States that the existing affiliate program converts demand that mostly already existed and is rarely incremental.
Uses incrementality, reaching buyers before intent exists, as the B2C sequencing driver.
Notes that creator/influencer disclosure rules are enforcement-backed and that the liability is the brand's as well as the creator's.
Flags retail/wholesale and distributor as the categories this efficiency order starves, rather than silently omitting them.
Names DTC versus retail versus marketplace cannibalization as the dominant governance risk, and requires the conflict check before any overlapping category's launch stage.
Attaches kill criteria to the creator stage including a performance or activation floor and a time-to-first-revenue window.

evals.prompt: Ostergaard Industrial Cloud, B2B, $31M ARR, enterprise-only: average deal $220k, nine-month cycles, and every single customer needs three to six months of configuration before go-live. We already run a 28-person professional services org that does all implementations today and sits at 90% utilization. On the partner side we have a referral track (proven, 52% activation) and 9 ISV integrations. Two partner managers. Which category next?
evals.expected_output: A sequence promoting SI/GSI to the front against the default efficiency order, justified by the already-staffed services arm and the implementer-led buyer route, with the services-org conflict sized and rules required before launch.
expectations: Promotes SI/GSI to the front of the sequence despite the default efficiency order ranking it near the back.
Names the existing 28-person services org as the reason: the standing job that makes SI/GSI expensive is already staffed and already carries the methodology.
States that the buyer's route to market outranks the effort ranking when the buyer purchases through implementers.
Notes that the default efficiency order starves SI/GSI and MSP, and names this user's specific promoting condition.
Treats the 90% services utilization as a capacity constraint rather than as spare capacity.

If the partner-services multiple is quoted ($7.13 of services per $1 of platform for services-heavy partners versus $1.26 for resell-focused), flags it as vendor-commissioned (Canalys for AWS) and directional only.
Names the conflict between an SI category and the in-house services org, and requires rules of engagement before that stage launches.
Lists SI/GSI readiness prerequisites that must exist: implementation methodology, certified-practitioner program, executive sponsorship, MSAs and sub-contracting terms.
Attaches an evidence-based gate to the SI stage requiring repeatable joint wins across multiple partners.
Opens one stage at a time and gates every later stage on the previous stage's evidence.
Keeps the output at category level and does not rank named consultancies.

evals.prompt: Piedmont Dispatch, B2B logistics SaaS, product-led, $99 to $899/mo self-serve, median time from signup to first value is 11 minutes, no onboarding call, no configuration. $7M ARR across about 4,000 paying accounts. Our new CRO came from an enterprise software company and wants a systems-integrator partner program plus an agency channel, because that's how they scaled at his last place. We have a public API and a growing set of third-party integrations. Two partner managers. Talk me through the sequence.
evals.expected_output: A sequence demoting SI/GSI and agency below marketplace because the product has no services gap, recommending ISV and marketplace instead, with the ego-system check applied and the CRO's precedent named as not being evidence.
expectations: States that a product needing no implementation demotes SI/GSI and agency below marketplace in the ranking.
Names the absence of a services gap as the reason neither SI/GSI nor agency has a job to do for this product.
Runs the ego-system check, asking what an SI or agency partner gains by joining now, and notes a category with no answer will sign logos and never activate.
Recommends the technology/ISV and/or marketplace categories ahead of the CRO's request.
Uses the existing public API and third-party integrations as the adjacency that makes the recommended stage cheap.
Deletes or defers SI/GSI with the constraint that ruled it out and a re-entry trigger, such as an enterprise tier shipping that requires configuration.
States plainly that the CRO's precedent from another company is not evidence for this product's sequence.
Presents 2-3 candidate sequences with trade-offs and a recommendation rather than a single unargued answer.
Argues the strongest case against its own recommended sequence before presenting it.
Attaches per-stage gates that open on evidence, with kill criteria including an activation floor and a rule for two consecutive missed quarters.
Costs each stage as a total loaded cost (headcount, enablement build, incentives, tooling, program spend), not as a headcount ask alone.

evals.prompt: We need a partner roadmap for Ashgrove Analytics (B2B data platform, $12M ARR, mid-market and up). Candidates on the table: Accenture, Slalom, a regional firm called Northpoint Data, Snowflake's partner network, and two boutique agencies we've worked with informally for a year. Rank these and tell me who to sign first and in what order, plus what the gates should be.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank the named companies with a handoff to the named-candidate prioritization sibling, followed by the same request answered at category level with readiness prerequisites, gates and a Not now list.
expectations: Declines to rank the named companies, stating this work is category-level sequencing only.
Routes the named-candidate ranking to the sibling skill for prioritizing named alliances (mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@alliance-prioritization).
Re-expresses the named candidates as the categories they belong to, such as SI/GSI, regional SI, technology/ISV or marketplace, and agency.
Produces a category sequence rather than a company sequence.
Asks for the current ecosystem picture (categories live today, partners per category, share active) before sequencing, or routes to the ecosystem-mapping sibling when none exists.
Names the efficiency ranking it used and states what that ranking starves.
Attaches readiness prerequisites per candidate category rather than per named firm.
Attaches per-stage gates with a pilot cohort shape, a partner-market-fit threshold of repeatable joint wins, and kill criteria.
Places at least one category in 'Not now' with a re-entry trigger.
States that the pilot cohort must receive full enablement, because a pilot starved of enablement tests nothing.

evals.prompt: Getting our MSP stage funded at Calderwood Telemetry (B2B observability, $16M ARR). Finance told me MDF is the easiest bucket to pull from: we already hold about 4% of channel revenue in MDF and it's underspent. So my ask is one partner manager's worth of time carved out of the existing team, plus $180k of MDF for partner marketing over four quarters. CFO wants the request expressed in headcount terms. Help me write the business case and the stage plan.
evals.expected_output: A business case that promotes headcount for this standing-job stage against the default funding-efficiency order, refuses the MDF-funded and headcount-framed asks, presents a total loaded cost, and writes MSP prerequisites, pilot shape and kill criteria before launch.
expectations: States the funding-mechanism efficiency order (program budget > MDF > headcount) and then promotes headcount for this stage because it opens a standing-job category.
States that MDF and program budget buy activity, never the standing capacity an MSP category runs on.
Warns that a standing job funded from a one-period budget fails at the second review.
Presents the ask as a total loaded cost covering salaries, enablement build, incentives, tooling and program spend.
Rejects the CFO's headcount framing, stating the request is for capital rather than enthusiasm.
Notes typical MDF utilization is only 40-60%, and flags the MDF sizing figures (2-6% of channel revenue, 25-50% cost-share per activity) as mixed vendor/analyst.
Names MDF's compliance cost: per-activity claims, proof-of-performance administration and audit rights.
Lists MSP readiness prerequisites and marks each met or missing: multi-tenant administration, monitoring and billing hooks, tiered support, support model, contracting.
States that MSP is a standing job both to stand up and to run, with slow time to first revenue.
Defines a pilot cohort with full enablement and an evidence gate before any scale investment.
Writes kill criteria before launch, including an activation floor near 20%, a time-to-first-deal window, and the two-consecutive-missed-quarters rule.
Names cross-functional sign-off owners (product, sales, finance, legal) rather than finance alone.

evals.prompt: We finished a full partner ecosystem map six weeks ago: every partner type we have, account overlap data pulled from our overlap tool, coverage gaps by segment and geography, the whole thing. Now my SVP wants to book a two-day offsite with sales, marketing, CS and product leadership to brainstorm which partner types we add next. Tarrant Systems, B2B infrastructure software, $27M ARR. Can you design the offsite agenda?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to start with the near-zero-cost map re-read and value blueprint rather than the two-day workshop, with the format efficiency order stated, the stopping rule given, and the condition that would genuinely promote the business-design workshop named.
expectations: States the facilitation-format efficiency order with the ecosystem-map re-read first and the business-design workshop last (map re-read > value blueprint > account mapping > partner persona > business-design workshop).
Recommends starting with a re-read of the existing map rather than rebuilding it or opening with the two-day workshop.
States the stopping rule: run from the top of the order and stop when the candidate pool stops changing.

Names the condition that would promote the two-day cross-functional business-design workshop: the answer would change how a GTM function operates day to day, such as comp plans, CS ownership or data sharing.
Notes that the existing account-overlap data makes the account-mapping session cheap, because the day or two of data work is already paid for.
Includes the value blueprint session and its ego-system check, drawn from the customer's position rather than the company's.
Names co-innovation risk and adoption-chain risk as the two risks the value blueprint surfaces.
Applies one question per message and does not batch questions.
Offers 2-3 candidate approaches with trade-offs and a recommendation at each real choice, then waits for the user.
Names assumptions aloud, including which category the room already wants and which capacity number is a guess.
Presents the deliverable section by section, validated one at a time, and gates finalization on the user's explicit approval.

evals.prompt: Setting up reporting for the agency partner category we launched 10 weeks ago at Wrenfield Commerce (B2B ecommerce ops platform, $21M ARR). 14 agencies signed so far. I want the dashboard to lead with category share of new revenue, since that's the number our board asks about, then partner NPS from a quarterly survey. Stage gate review is in 8 weeks. What should I instrument and what should the gate read?
evals.expected_output: An instrumentation plan led by activation rate and time-to-first-deal, refusing category share of new revenue as the stage-gate read and naming the funding-decision condition that would promote it, with NPS demoted and the gate threshold set on repeatable joint wins.
expectations: States the KPI instrumentation efficiency order with partner activation rate first (activation rate > time-to-first-deal > partner-sourced pipeline > enablement completion == deal-registration volume > category share of new revenue > partner NPS).
Declines to lead the stage-gate read with category share of new revenue, stating it needs roughly a year of cohorts before it says anything.
Names the condition that does promote category share of new revenue: a funding or board decision rather than a stage gate.
States partner NPS is opinion, useful for diagnosing a failing cohort but never sufficient to open a gate.
Defines partner activation rate as signed partners closing at least one deal, and makes it the gate's first read.
Adds time-to-first-deal measured against the expected window for the agency category.
Adds enablement or certification completion inside the onboarding window, noting the 90-120 day window with its ANALYST (Forrester) flag.
Sets the gate threshold as repeatable joint wins across multiple partners rather than a single first win.
Names the gate outcome vocabulary: pass-and-scale, extend-pilot once with a named fix, re-scope, or kill.
Warns that 100% gate survival suggests soft gates while 0% suggests a broken candidate pool.
Sets gate thresholds from the company's own base rates where any exist, using published figures only to sanity-check.

evals.prompt: Hollenbeck Data, B2B data-quality platform, $48M ARR. We run six partner categories now: referral, affiliate, ISV, agency, two hyperscaler marketplaces, and a reseller tier we added 18 months ago. Partner-sourced revenue has been flat at roughly $9.4M for five straight quarters while my team went from 3 to 7 partner managers, and we bought a PRM platform last year that nobody really uses. Exec team wants an MSP category added for FY28 and is also talking about cutting the agency tier to free up headcount. What's the right sequence?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to add nothing and deepen instead, reading the flat revenue against rising coordination cost as the inverted-U signal with academic provenance, refusing the MSP addition, and treating the proposed agency cut as an equally high-risk subtraction.
expectations: Recommends adding no new category now, and deepening the existing ones instead.
Identifies the inverted-U signal: coordination cost rising (3 to 7 partner managers) while total partner-sourced revenue flattens.
Cites the alliance-portfolio-diversity inverted-U research and flags it ACADEMIC, for example Jiang, Tao & Santoro 2010 in Strategic Management Journal or the Lee et al. 2017 meta-analysis.
States that this research argues for restraint and sequencing but prescribes no order.
States it is the field's only independent, non-self-interested evidence base.
Declines to open the MSP category for FY28, or gates it behind the freeze lifting with a named trigger.
Treats cutting the agency tier as high-risk as adding a category, requiring the conflict and dependency to be sized before shrinking that route.
Names over-rotation on one category while cutting others as a documented failure pattern, not a neutral cost saving.
Names the PRM platform nobody uses as tooling bought ahead of the workflow that needed it, sitting as compliance theater rather than as capacity.
Reads per-category activation before deciding anything, rather than treating the flat $9.4M as a single aggregate.
Names category sprawl followed by forced pruning as the pattern this ecosystem is already in.
Sets a review cadence and explicit re-sequencing triggers, such as a gate result, a category's activation collapsing, a product-readiness slip, a conflict incident or a market shift.
